\chapter{Peace and Welcome}
\label{ch:pa-peace-and-welcome}
\hlchaptermodality{34}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can greet with salam and welcome someone with ji aaian nu, name the three-consonant Arabic root that salam shares with islam and muslim, say where the postposition nu stands, and write salam in Gurmukhi.}

The reader welcomes an arrival, translates the phrase piece by piece into life, those who have come, and to, states that nu follows the word it marks rather than preceding it, and writes salam now that its looped letter has been traced.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[salām]{salām — the third hello, and the one that means peace}

\label{lesson:PA-C34-salaam}



\begin{quote}
Two greetings opened this book: \emph{sat srī akāl}, the Sikh one, and \emph{namaste}, the shared one. Two words for thanks followed: \emph{dhannavād} and \emph{shukrīā}, one from each tradition. The greetings have been waiting for their third.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\emph{salām} — \textbf{peace}, said as a greeting
\end{quote}

Two even syllables, the second longer: \emph{sa-lām}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Salām} is Arabic \emph{salām}, \textquotedblleft{}peace, safety, wholeness.\textquotedblright{} Arabic builds words on skeletons of three consonants, and this one is \textbf{s-l-m}. Pour different vowels into that skeleton and you get:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{salām}, peace;
  \item \emph{islām}, submission, the act of giving oneself over;
  \item \emph{muslim}, the one who does it;
  \item and, across the family line in Hebrew, \emph{shalom}, the same three consonants with a sound shift and the same meaning.
\end{itemize}

The \textbf{\pa{ਮਦਦ}} of \textquotedblleft{}to help\textquotedblright{} and the previous session's \textbf{\pa{ਮਾਫ਼}} came into Punjabi by the same road. This one arrived on the same road and became a greeting rather than a noun.

Punjab is split between two states and two scripts, and \emph{salām} is the everyday hello across its western half, where \emph{sat srī akāl} is the everyday hello in the east. A learner who can say all three can greet anyone in the region without guessing at their tradition first — which is what this book has been building toward since its opening page.

On the page \emph{salām} needs one letter still to come. It arrives next session.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{salām} — peace
  \item \emph{Run through:} all three greetings — \emph{sat srī akāl}, \emph{namaste}, \emph{salām}
  \item \emph{State:} the three consonants of the Arabic root (\emph{s-l-m})
  \item \emph{Name:} two other words built on that root (\emph{islām}, \emph{muslim})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the greeting that means peace. (\emph{Salām}.) Which three greetings can you now choose between? (\emph{Sat srī akāl}, \emph{namaste}, \emph{salām}.) What does the root mean? (Peace, wholeness.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A8\%B8\%E0\%A8\%B2\%E0\%A8\%BE\%E0\%A8\%AE}{Wiktionary: salam}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D8\%B3\%D9\%84\%D8\%A7\%D9\%85}{Wiktionary: salam (Arabic)}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la]{\pa{ਲ} — the last piece of a four-letter greeting}

\label{lesson:PA-W09-lalla}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\pa{ਸ}} and \textbf{\pa{ਮ}} once each. Say \emph{salām} aloud. Of its four letters you can already write three; one is missing.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — one letter}
Trace \textbf{\pa{ਲ}} twice and say \emph{la}. A loop that starts at the top line, drops, and comes back up to meet it.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Cover the model. Write \textbf{\pa{ਲ}} once. Compare only whether the loop closes back on the top line.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Four letters, four shapes you can now form. The word is assembled one session after next.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jī āiāṁ nū̃]{jī āiāṁ nū̃ — a welcome built from three things you own}

\label{lesson:PA-C34-ji-aaian-nu}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\pa{ਜੀ}} once. Say \emph{āuṇā}, \textquotedblleft{}to come,\textquotedblright{} from the six core verbs. Say \emph{mainū̃ panjābī pasand hai} from the liking lesson. Every piece of this session's phrase is already in your mouth; nothing here is new except the joining.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one phrase}
\begin{quote}
\emph{jī āiāṁ nū̃} — \textbf{welcome}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
Three pieces, and you have met all three.

\textbf{\pa{ਜੀ}} is the word from the start of this chapter run, the one usually traced to Sanskrit \emph{jīva}, \textquotedblleft{}life\textquotedblright{} — the same \emph{jīva} whose Indo-European root also stands behind Latin \emph{vīvus}. It sits here beside \emph{salām}, whose own root \textbf{s-l-m} the last session opened; two greetings, two traditions, one page.

\emph{Āiāṁ} is a past form of \emph{āuṇā}, \textquotedblleft{}to come,\textquotedblright{} the verb built earlier out of Sanskrit \emph{āgacchati} — \textquotedblleft{}go\textquotedblright{} with \emph{ā-} \textquotedblleft{}toward\textquotedblright{} glued on the front. The ending here means \emph{those who have come}, more than one of them, and respectful.

\emph{Nū̃} is a small word placed \textbf{after} the thing it marks, not before it. It points at the person something is aimed at. It was used inside \emph{mainū̃} without stopping to name it; here it gets its name. English would put \emph{to} in front; Punjabi puts \emph{nū̃} behind.

Read in Punjabi order the phrase says: \textbf{to those who have come — life}. The host wishes life on the arrivals. English \emph{welcome} is built from an old \emph{wil-}, \textquotedblleft{}pleasure,\textquotedblright{} and \emph{-cuma}, \textquotedblleft{}guest,\textquotedblright{} and names the guest instead.

On the page two of these pieces still wait for letters. \textbf{\pa{ਜੀ}} you can already write, and the rest arrives shortly.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Writing: assemble \pa{ਸਲਾਮ}}
The looped letter has been traced, so the greeting from two sessions back can be built. Four moves: \textbf{\pa{ਸ}}, \textbf{\pa{ਲ}}, the upright \textbf{\pa{ਾ}}, \textbf{\pa{ਮ}}. Written out: \textbf{\pa{ਸਲਾਮ}}.

Copy it once with the model visible, saying \emph{salām} as you finish. Cover the model, write it once more, and compare only whether the upright falls after the second letter rather than the first.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{jī āiāṁ nū̃} — welcome
  \item \emph{Translate:} the phrase piece by piece (life; those who have come; to)
  \item \emph{State:} where \emph{nū̃} stands relative to the word it marks (after it)
  \item \emph{Greet:} someone with \emph{salām}, then welcome them in
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Welcome someone. (\emph{Jī āiāṁ nū̃}.) Which verb is \emph{āiāṁ} a form of? (\emph{Āuṇā}.) Where does \emph{nū̃} stand? (After.) Write \textbf{\pa{ਸਲਾਮ}} once from memory.

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A8\%86\%E0\%A8\%89\%E0\%A8\%A3\%E0\%A8\%BE}{Wiktionary: auna}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A8\%A8\%E0\%A9\%82\%E0\%A9\%B0}{Wiktionary: nu}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[aa]{\pa{ਆ} — a letter you can already build}

\label{lesson:PA-W09-aara}



\begin{quote}
Write the standalone \textbf{\pa{ਅ}} once. Then write the upright stroke \textbf{\pa{ਾ}} that lengthens a vowel — the one that turned \textbf{\pa{ਹ}} into \textbf{\pa{ਹਾ}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — one letter}
Put the two together and you have \textbf{\pa{ਆ}}, the standalone long \emph{ā}. Trace it twice. This is the shape a word starting with \emph{ā-} opens on, where \textbf{\pa{ਅ}} opens a word starting with short \emph{a-}.

Nothing new has to be memorised here: two shapes you already own, standing side by side and read as one letter.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Cover the models. Write \textbf{\pa{ਅ}}, then \textbf{\pa{ਆ}}. Compare only the added upright.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
A letter built from two you had already climbed.
\end{tcolorbox}
